title: Oil Hits $100 Again as Houthi Threats Open a Second Front in Energy Crisis
excerpt: Brent crude breached the $100-a-barrel threshold for the first time since May as Yemen's Houthis targeted Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, adding a second chokepoint to the Strait of Hormuz disruption and pushing U.S. gas prices above $4 a gallon.
body:
• Brent crude topped $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May after Houthi rebels struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, threatening a second maritime chokepoint alongside the Strait of Hormuz.
  • U.S. gasoline prices have climbed back above $4 a gallon, with diesel at $5.21 — a 39% year-over-year increase that ripples through freight and food costs.
  • Oil is up nearly 40% in July alone, reviving stagflation fears and pushing the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.7%, its highest close since January 2025.
  • The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve sits at 316.5 million barrels, its lowest since 1983, leaving limited buffers against further supply shocks.

Brent crude oil surged past $100 a barrel on Thursday after Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed strikes on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, opening a second front in the energy supply disruption that has roiled global markets since the U.S.-Iran conflict erupted in late February.

The breach of the triple-digit mark — the first since May — came as West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, shot up 6.2% to $92.19 a barrel, according to the Wall Street Journal. Oil has gained nearly 40% in July, its steepest monthly climb since March.

At the pump, the pain is immediate. National average gasoline prices pushed back above $4 a gallon this week, according to AAA, erasing relief from a brief U.S.-Iran ceasefire in June. Diesel stands at $5.21 a gallon — up 39% year-over-year — driving up costs for trucking, construction and agriculture.

From One Chokepoint to Two

The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20% of global oil flowed before the conflict, has been effectively closed since Iran resumed attacks on commercial shipping after the June ceasefire collapsed. Now, Houthi threats to vessels exiting the Red Sea through the Bab el-Mandeb strait have compounded the disruption.

Al Jazeera reported that two large Saudi tankers reversed course and returned to port on Tuesday. If the Bab el-Mandeb closes, Saudi Arabia's ability to move its 7 million barrels per day to market would be severely constrained — the Suez Canal cannot accommodate the largest crude tankers.

"You can't have it both ways. If there is a war in the Middle East and the Strait of Hormuz is effectively closed, prices are going to be high."

— U.S. oil company executives in calls with the Trump administration, according to the Wall Street Journal

Supply Buffers Running Thin

The cushions that absorbed the initial price shock in March are disappearing. U.S. crude stocks have fallen for a third straight month — more than 60 million barrels withdrawn over 12 weeks, according to Energy Information Administration data. Gasoline inventories sit 6% below the five-year seasonal average.

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve, at 316.5 million barrels, is at its lowest since 1983 and more than 415 million barrels below capacity. Chinese refineries have resumed large-scale crude purchases, and bipartisan legislation to expand sanctions on Russia's energy sector could remove yet more barrels from the global market.

Markets Flash Stagflation Warning

The energy shock rattled financial markets on Thursday. The 10-year Treasury yield topped 4.7%, its highest close since January 2025. The Dow and S&P 500 each fell about 1%, while the Nasdaq dropped more than 2%. Mortgage rates climbed to 6.58%, with some economists warning 7% looms.

"Stagflation risk has been very much there for each economy since March, in different ways. The latest broadening of the conflict increases the risk of stagflation for sure."

— Alessia Berardi, Head of Global Macroeconomics, Amundi Investment Institute

Markets now price in roughly two more Federal Reserve rate hikes by January, according to Reuters. New U.S. tariffs on goods from 60 trading partners are layering additional inflationary pressure. The World Bank's chief economist warned the conflict could knock global growth to 1.3%, down from 2.9% last year.

India and the Diaspora Feel the Squeeze

Energy-importing economies in South and Southeast Asia are particularly exposed. India, which imports roughly 85% of its crude and sources a large share from the Gulf, faces mounting pressure on its fuel subsidy bill and current account deficit. Higher crude costs feed directly into petrol, diesel and cooking gas prices, driving food and transportation inflation across the country.

For Indian-Americans, the squeeze runs both ways: higher pump prices at home in the U.S., and costlier essentials for family in India.

What Comes Next

The White House maintains military operations will eventually restore oil flows. "Oil and gas prices will plummet back to pre-conflict levels," spokesperson Taylor Rogers said. Analysts are less sanguine. With reserves depleted, inventories declining and two critical maritime routes under threat, the supply-side arithmetic points to sustained upward pressure — barring a diplomatic breakthrough that has proved elusive. For now, $4-a-gallon gas looks more like a floor than a ceiling.
nri_angle: India, a major oil importer sourcing most crude from the Gulf, faces mounting fuel costs and inflation from the dual chokepoint disruption, while Indian-Americans feel the squeeze at the pump.
